accepted.question_text: Investigate how the subtraction set in a subtraction game determines the length and structure of the eventual period, and extend the same question to partizan subtraction games where the two players have different subtraction sets.

evidence.quote: Subtraction games are known to be periodic. Investigate the relationship between the subtraction set and the length and structure of the period. (For subtraction games, see WW, pp.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether every finite octal game is ultimately periodic, resolve additional outstanding concrete octal codes, find an octal game with period longer than 149459, and explain the structure of periods in games already known to be periodic.

evidence.quote: Are all finite octal games ultimately periodic? (See WW, pp. 81–115, [Guy 1996, Section 4], p. 67 in this volume. Such games are defined by a code d0 ·d1 d2 d3 . . . .

accepted.question_text: Study hexadecimal take-and-break games and determine conditions under which they are arithmetically periodic.

evidence.quote: Examine some hexadecimal games (games with code digits dk in the interval from 0 to 15 = F: see WW, pp. 115–116, and the last three examples in the table on page 67 of this book). Obtain conditions for arithmetic periodicity.

accepted.question_text: Extend the analysis of Domineering to larger boards, including characterizing hot positions up to infinitesimal shift and finding positions with temperatures not already known.

evidence.quote: Extend the analysis of Domineering to larger boards. (Left and Right take turns to place dominoes on a checker-board. Left orients her dominoes NorthSouth and Right orients his East-West.

accepted.question_text: Analyze positions in the game of Go.

evidence.quote: Analyze positions in the game of Go. (Compare [Berlekamp and Wolfe 1994; Berlekamp and Kim 1996; Landman 1996].)

accepted.question_text: Determine the least board length n for which Four-in-a-row on a 4×n board is a first-player win.

evidence.quote: In an earlier edition of this paper I asked if Go-Moku (Five-in-a-row, GoBang, Pegotty) is a win for the first player.

accepted.question_text: Complete the analysis of impartial Eatcakes, especially the remoteness behavior for fixed breadth and large length.

evidence.quote: Complete the analysis of impartial Eatcakes. (See WW, pp. 269, 271, 276– 277. Eatcakes is an example of a join or selective compound of games. Each player plays in all the component games.

accepted.question_text: Complete the analysis of Hotcakes for integer-sided rectangles beyond the small cases already understood.

evidence.quote: Complete the analysis of Hotcakes. (See WW, pp. 279–282. Also played with integer-sided rectangles, but as a union or selective compound in which each player moves in some of the components.

accepted.question_text: Develop a misère theory for unions of partizan games, where a move may be made in as many component games as desired and the last player to move loses.

evidence.quote: Develop a misère theory for unions of partizan games. (In a union of two or more games, you move in as many component games as you wish. In misère play, the last player loses.)

accepted.question_text: Extend the analysis of Squares Off, the heap game where a move removes a perfect square greater than 1 from any number of heaps with special terminal effects for heaps of size 0, 1, 2, and 3.

evidence.quote: Extend the analysis of Squares Off. (See WW, pp. 299. Played with heaps of beans. A move is to take a perfect square (> 1) number of beans from any number of heaps. Heaps of 0, 1, 2 or 3 cannot be further reduced.

accepted.question_text: Extend the analysis of Top Entails and explain the loony positions that appear at unexpectedly large stack sizes.

evidence.quote: Extend the analysis of Top Entails. (WW, pp. 376–377. Played with stacks of coins. Either split a stack into two smaller ones, or remove the top coin from a stack. In the latter case your opponent’s move must use the same stack. Last player wins.

accepted.question_text: Extend the analysis of All Square, where splitting a heap into two perfect-square heaps forces the same player to move again.

evidence.quote: Extend the analysis of All Square. (WW, pp. 385. This game involves complimenting moves after which the same player has an extra bonus move. Note that this happens in Dots-and-Boxes when a box is completed. All Square is played with heaps of beans.

accepted.question_text: Analyze the misère version of finite octal games and develop methods that go beyond the already solved case of misère Kayles.

evidence.quote: Analyze the misère version of the octal games of Problem 2. (See [Allemang 1984] and WW, pp. 411–421.) William L. Sibert made a breakthrough by completing the analysis of misère Kayles; see the postscript to [Sibert and Conway 1992].

accepted.question_text: For Moebius, determine whether the remarkable pattern seen at 18 coins persists for larger numbers of coins and estimate the growth rate of the nim-values.

evidence.quote: Moebius, when played on 18 coins has a remarkable pattern. Is there any trace of pattern for larger numbers of coins? Can any estimate be made for the rate of growth of the nim-values? (Played with a row of coins.

accepted.question_text: For Mogul, determine whether the striking patterns seen at 24 coins and echoes at 40, 56, and 64 coins persist at larger sizes or whether the game eventually becomes chaotic.

evidence.quote: Mogul has an even more striking pattern when played on 24 coins, which has some echoes when played on 40, 56 or 64 coins. Thereafter, is there complete chaos? (See Problem 14. A move turns 1, 2, . . . , 7 coins.)

accepted.question_text: Find an analysis of Antonim with four or more coins.

evidence.quote: Find an analysis of Antonim with four or more coins. (WW, pp. 459–462. Played with coins on a strip of squares. A move moves a coin from one square to a smaller-numbered square. Only one coin to a square, except that square zero can have any number of coins.

accepted.question_text: Extend the analysis of Kotzig’s Nim, decide whether every finite move set gives eventual periodicity as the circle length grows, and analyze the misère version.

evidence.quote: Extend the analysis of Kotzig’s Nim. (WW, pp. 481–483. Players alternately place coins on a circular strip, at most one coin on a square.

accepted.question_text: Obtain asymptotic estimates for the proportions of N-, O-, and P-positions in Epstein’s Put-or-Take-a-Square game.

evidence.quote: Obtain asymptotic estimates for the proportions of N-, O- and P-positions in Epstein’s Put-or-Take-a-Square game. (WW, pp. 484–486. Played with one heap of beans.

accepted.question_text: Analyze Tribulations, the triangular-number analogue of Put-or-Take-a-Square, and test Norton’s conjectures that there are no O-positions and that N-positions outnumber P-positions in the golden ratio.

evidence.quote: Simon Norton’s game of Tribulations is similar to Epstein’s game, but squares are replaced by triangular numbers. Norton conjectures that there are no O-positions, and that the N-positions outnumber the P-positions in golden ratio. True up to 5000 beans.

accepted.question_text: Complete the analysis of D.U.D.E.N.E.Y. and determine whether a persistent small fraction of odd parameter values always remains unresolved.

evidence.quote: Complete the analysis of D.U.D.E.N.E.Y. (Played with a single heap of beans. Either player may take any number of beans from 1 to Y , except that the immediately previous move mustn’t be repeated. When you can’t move you lose.

accepted.question_text: Analyze Schuhstrings, the D.U.D.E.N.E.Y. variant in which a deduction of zero is also allowed but may not be repeated immediately.

evidence.quote: Schuhstrings is the same as D.U.D.E.N.E.Y., except that a deduction of zero is also allowed, but cannot be immediately repeated (WW, pp. 489–490).

accepted.question_text: Analyze nonrepeating Nim under the medium-local, short-local, long-local, short-global, and long-global nonrepetition rules.

evidence.quote: Analyze nonrepeating Nim, in which neither player is allowed to repeat a move. Assume that b beans have been taken from heap H, and pick your variant: medium local : b beans may not be taken from heap H until some other move is made in heap H.

accepted.question_text: Analyze Burning-the-Candle-at-Both-Ends Nim and the related Hub-and-Spoke Nim variants.

evidence.quote: Burning-the-Candle-at-Both-Ends. John Conway and Aviezri Fraenkel ask us to analyze Nim played with a row of heaps. A move may only be made in the leftmost or in the rightmost heap. Of course, when a heap becomes empty, its neighbor becomes the end heap.

accepted.question_text: Continue the analysis of The Princess and the Roses.

evidence.quote: Continue the analysis of The Princess and the Roses. (WW, pp. 490– 494. Played with heaps of beans. Take one bean, or two beans, one from each of two different heaps. The rules seem trivially simple, but the analysis takes on remarkable ramifications.)

accepted.question_text: Analyze Sprouts with seven or more spots and the misère form with five or more spots.

evidence.quote: Analyze the Conway–Paterson game of Sprouts with seven or more spots, or the misère form with five or more spots. (WW, pp. 564–568. A move joins two spots, or a spot to itself by a curve that doesn’t meet any other spot or previously drawn curve.

accepted.question_text: Extend the analysis of Sylver Coinage.

evidence.quote: Extend the analysis of Sylver Coinage. (WW, pp. 575–597. Players alternately name different positive integers, but may not name a number that is the sum of previously named ones, with repetitions allowed. Whoever names 1 loses.

accepted.question_text: Extend the analysis of Chomp, including the first complete analysis of 3D-Chomp.

evidence.quote: Extend the analysis of Chomp. (WW, pp. 598–599. Players alternately name divisors of N , which may not be multiples of previously named numbers.

accepted.question_text: Extend the diforest analysis of von Neumann’s game to directed acyclic graphs.

evidence.quote: Extend Uléhla’s or Berlekamp’s analysis of von Neumann’s game from diforests to directed acyclic graphs (WW, pp. 570–572; [Uléhla 1980]).

accepted.question_text: Prove that Black does not have a forced win in Chess.

evidence.quote: Prove that Black doesn’t have a forced win in Chess.

accepted.question_text: In the quarter-infinite-board position WKa1, WRb2, BKc3, decide whether White can force a win, in how many moves, and what the smallest winning finite board is under the edge-escape rule for Black.

evidence.quote: A King and Rook versus King problem. Played on a quarter-infinite board, with initial position WKa1, WRb2 and BKc3. Can White win? If so, in how few moves?

accepted.question_text: Determine for which initial positions Lion can catch Man in Gale’s quadrant game, and analyze the wedge-region variation.

evidence.quote: David Gale’s version of Lion and Man. L and M are confined to the nonnegative quadrant of the plane. They move alternately a distance of at most one unit. For which initial positions can L catch M? Conjecture: L wins if he is northeast of M.

accepted.question_text: Solve Gale’s Vingt-et-un and determine which player wins under the stated card-selection rules.

evidence.quote: Gale’s Vingt-et-un. Cards numbered 1 through 10 are laid on the table. L chooses a card. Then R chooses cards until his total of chosen cards exceeds the card chosen by L. Then L chooses until her cumulative total exceeds that of R, etc.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether Subset Take-away is always a second-player win, as conjectured by Gale.

evidence.quote: Subset Take-away. Given a finite set, players alternately choose proper subsets subject to the rule that, once a subset has been chosen, none of its subsets may be chosen later by either player. Last player wins.

accepted.question_text: Develop a theory of Cannibal Games or solve important special families of positions on finite digraphs.

evidence.quote: Eggleton and Fraenkel ask for a theory of Cannibal Games or an analysis of special families of positions. They are played on an arbitrary finite digraph. Place any numbers of “cannibals” on any vertices.

accepted.question_text: For Welter’s Game on an arbitrary digraph, make a dictionary of P-positions and formulate winning strategies for the other positions.

evidence.quote: Welter’s Game on an arbitrary digraph. Place a number of monochromatic tokens on distinct vertices of a directed acyclic graph. A token may be moved to any unoccupied immediate follower. Last player wins.

accepted.question_text: For Restricted Positrons and Electrons on a Welter strip, formulate winning strategies when they exist and analyze the misère version as well.

evidence.quote: Restricted Positrons and Electrons. Fraenkel places a number of Positrons (Pink tokens) and Electrons (Ebony tokens) on distinct vertices of a Welter strip.

accepted.question_text: Analyze the general Positrons and Electrons game on arbitrary digraphs.

evidence.quote: General Positrons and Electrons. Like 36, but played on an arbitrary digraph. Last player wins.

accepted.question_text: Generalize the analysis of Fulves’s Merger beyond the specific 1,2,3,4,5,6,7 starting position and understand related parity-target variants.

evidence.quote: Fulves’s Merger. Karl Fulves, Box 433, Teaneck NJ 07666, sent the following game. Start with heaps of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 beans.

accepted.question_text: Analyze sowing or Mancala-style games, especially the African sowing move and related partizan and impartial variants.

evidence.quote: Sowing or Mancala Games. Kraitchik [1941, p. 282] describes Ruma, which he attributes to Mr. Punga. Bell and Cornelius [1988, pp.

accepted.question_text: Find chess endgames with new combinatorial game values beyond the ones already known.

evidence.quote: Chess again. Noam Elkies [1996] has found endgames with values 0, 1, 12 , ∗, ↑, ↑∗, ⇑ ∗, etc. Find endgames with new values. (See also Problems 29, 30 and 45.)

accepted.question_text: Develop a coherent theory of poset-indexed game compounds G(P), generalizing both sequential compounds and disjunctive sums.

evidence.quote: Sequential compounds of games have been studied by Stromquist and Ullman [1993]. They mention a more general compound. Let (P, <) be a finite poset and for each x ∈ P let Gx be a game. Consider a game G(P ) played as follows.

accepted.question_text: In Beanstalk, decide whether Jack can always win when the Giant starts from any odd integer greater than 1; in Beans-Don’t-Talk, decide whether any O-positions of infinite remoteness exist.

evidence.quote: Beanstalk and Beans-Don’t-Talk are games invented by John Isbell and by John Conway [Guy 1986]. Beanstalk is played between Jack and the Giant. The Giant chooses a positive integer, n0 . Then J. and G. play alternately n1 , n2 , n3 , . . .

accepted.question_text: Analyze Inverting Hackenbush and its tree generalization, where cutting an edge is followed by turning the remaining position upside down and replanting it.

evidence.quote: Inverting Hackenbush. John Conway turns Hackenbush (described on page 56 in this volume) into a hot game by amending the move to ‘remove an edge of your color and everything thus disconnected from the ground, and then turn the remaining string upside-down and...

accepted.question_text: Analyze Konane further, especially the appearance of infinitesimals and hot values of arbitrarily high temperature.

evidence.quote: Konane [Ernst and Berlekamp]. There is much to be discovered about this fascinating and eminently playable game, which exhibits the values 0, ∗, ∗2, ↑, 2−n , and many other infinitesimals and also hot values of arbitrarily high temperature.

accepted.question_text: Determine the habitat of the value ∗2, particularly whether it occurs in Chilled Go, Domineering, and 8×8 Chess.

evidence.quote: Elwyn Berlekamp asks: ‘What is the habitat of ∗2?’ This value, defined as {0, ∗ | 0, ∗}, does not occur in Blockbusting, Hackenbush, Col or Go. It does occur in Konane and 6 × 6 Chess. What about Chilled Go, Domineering and 8 × 8 Chess?

accepted.question_text: Analyze two-dimensional Nim variants on rectangular, triangular, and hexagonal boards, including the contiguous-heaps restriction.

evidence.quote: There are various ways of playing two-dimensional Nim. One form is discussed on p. 313 of WW. Another is proposed by Berman, Fraenkel and Kahane in Problem 41, Discrete Math. 45 (1983), 137–138. Start with a rectangular array of heaps of beans.

accepted.question_text: For disconnected polyominoes of the types shown in the source, determine whether they tile rectangles and, if so, find the smallest such rectangles.

evidence.quote: Many results are known concerning tiling rectangles with polyominoes. One can extend such problems to disconnected polyominoes. For instance, can a rectangle be tiled by 22 22 ? By 22 22 2 ? If so, what are the smallest rectangles that can be so tiled?

accepted.question_text: Find all binary words that can be reduced to one peg in one-dimensional Peg Solitaire.

evidence.quote: Find all words that can be reduced to one peg in one-dimensional Peg Solitaire. (A move is for a peg to jump over an adjacent peg into an empty adjacent space, and remove the jumped-over peg: for instance, 1101 → 0011 → 0100, where 1 represents a peg and 0 an...

accepted.question_text: Find a simple, playable game with an intricate explicit solution that is provably NP-hard or harder.

evidence.quote: Elwyn Berlekamp asks if there is a game that has simple, playable rules, an intricate explicit solution, and is provably NP or harder.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether Four-File is a draw.

evidence.quote: John Selfridge asks: is Four-File a draw? Four-File is played on a chessboard with the chess pieces in their usual starting positions, but only on the a-, c-, e- and g-files (a rook, a bishop, a king, a knight and four pawns on each side).

accepted.question_text: Develop a complete theory of closed 1×n Dots-and-Boxes, prove additional nimber decomposition theorems, and compile a database of nim-values.

evidence.quote: Elwyn Berlekamp asks for a complete theory of closed 1 × n Dots-andBoxes, those with starting position r r r r r r r r r r r r r r r r r r r r A sample position is r r r r r r r r r r r r r r r r r r r r (See WW, Chapter 16.) Are there more nimber decompositio...

accepted.question_text: Explain how to play sums of games with varied overheating operators and find a simple relation between the operator parameters and the resulting game.

evidence.quote: Berlekamp notes that overheating operators provide a very concise way of expressing closed-form solutions to many games, and David Moews observes that monotonicity and linearity depend on the parameters and the domain.
